notes_context:
Memory items from past tasks:
- [rb-0003] Guard division by zero for empty collections: The weighted average must return zero when the invoice has no lines or zero total quantity.
  Compute the denominator first and return the zero constant early when it is falsy, then perform the weighted sum with an explicit ZERO start value so empty inputs never raise ZeroDivisionError.
- [rb-0001] Round monetary results with the project's money helper: The first attempt returned an unrounded Decimal division and was rejected for violating the team's rounding convention.
  When a function returns a money amount, wrap the final value in the repository's rounding helper (e.g. ledgerly.money.round_money) rather than returning a raw Decimal division or using Python's round()/quantize(), which use banker's rounding.
- [rb-0004] Reuse existing error and money helpers for validation: When implementing a new function in a codebase with established helpers, mirror the existing patterns for errors and money handling rather than inventing new ones.
  Read sibling functions (e.g. issue_invoice) first to learn the project's error codes and helper functions. Reuse BillingError with the same code strings and to_money/round_money/ZERO for monetary validation and rounding so behavior stays consistent.
- [rb-0002] Read the money module before implementing money logic: Inspecting ledgerly/money.py revealed ZERO, round_money and to_money, which the accepted solution reused.
  Before writing arithmetic on prices or totals, open the project's money module and reuse its constants and helpers (ZERO, to_money, round_money) so behavior matches existing functions like line_total and invoice_total.
- [rb-0005] Guard bool when validating integer inputs: Python's bool is a subclass of int, so isinstance(x, int) accepts True/False; explicitly reject bools for positive-integer checks.
  Use `isinstance(quantity, bool) or not isinstance(quantity, int) or quantity <= 0` to reject booleans and non-positive values. This prevents True being silently accepted as quantity 1.
- [rb-0006] Inspect models and tests before implementing: Reading dataclass definitions and existing tests up front clarifies field names, defaults, and expected return semantics, reducing rework.
  Before writing code, cat models.py, errors.py, and relevant tests to confirm constructor signatures (e.g. LineItem(description, quantity, unit_price)) and how the function will be called. This avoids mismatched argument order or wrong status field names.

item.title: Reuse existing period-arithmetic helpers and conventions
item.description: Before implementing a new date/period function, read sibling modules for established helpers and error conventions and mirror them.
item.content: Inspect related modules (e.g. subscriptions.py, clock.py, errors.py) first: reuse ensure_utc for timezone normalization and BillingError with a short code for invalid input, so the new function behaves consistently with the rest of the library.

item.title: Compute strictly-after renewal with floor division plus one
item.description: For periodic events anchored at a start time, the first occurrence strictly after a timestamp is start + ((after - start) // length + 1) * length.
item.content: Handle the before-start case separately (return start + length, since the start itself is not a renewal), then use integer floor division on timedeltas to get the index and add one. This avoids off-by-one errors when `after` lands exactly on a renewal.

item.title: Validate period_days defensively, excluding bool
item.description: Guard against non-positive or non-integer period_days, remembering that bool is a subclass of int in Python.
item.content: Check `isinstance(period_days, int) and not isinstance(period_days, bool) and period_days > 0` before building the timedelta, raising BillingError('invalid_period', ...) otherwise; this prevents zero-division and silently wrong schedules.
